cards.front: Recall a key point about African and Caribbean Fusion Music
cards.back: Polyrhythm (multiple conflicting rhythmic patterns simultaneously) is central to African music — it creates complex, layered rhythmic textures.

cards.front: Recall a key point about African and Caribbean Fusion Music
cards.back: Caribbean genres each have distinct rhythmic signatures: reggae (off-beat skank guitar, one-drop drumming), ska (fast off-beat), calypso (syncopated melody).

cards.front: Recall a key point about African and Caribbean Fusion Music
cards.back: Cyclic structures repeat musical patterns — unlike Western through-composed forms, African music often builds intensity through cyclical repetition and layering.

cards.front: Recall a key point about African and Caribbean Fusion Music
cards.back: Afrobeat (Fela Kuti) combines West African highlife with jazz, funk and Yoruba music — it demonstrates how fusion creates entirely new genres.

cards.front: What should you know about music exam tips?
cards.back: Name rhythmic devices precisely (polyrhythm, cross-rhythm, skank, off-beat). Explain cyclic structure. Identify specific Caribbean genre features. Compare fusion approaches.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: African and Caribbean music is just drumming with no structure. Correct: African and Caribbean music has sophisticated structures: polyrhythm, cyclic patterns, call and response, and specific rhythmic cells (clave, tumbao, skank). These are identifiable, nameable features using AQA vocabulary. The exam expects precise analytical terminology.
Compare the rhythmic features of an African drumming piece with a reggae track. Identify at least four rhythmic terms from the AQA list and explain their effect.

cards.back: In the AQA GCSE Music listening exam, questions about african and caribbean fusion music typically ask you to: identify features by ear; describe how they are used; explain their effect; compare features between extracts.
